title: Data Centers Divide Democrats in Michigan Primary
author: Drop Site News
content:

post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe6a6cd04-8866-4d27-a206-2cd0f5312b1c_1200x801.jpeg)A
demonstrator at an April rally in Traverse City, Michigan, holds a sign
emblematic of the growing data center resistance. _(Miles MacClure)_

_Story by Miles MacClure_

Over the past year, dim, windowless, gargantuan warehouses have taken center
stage in rural Michigan. The data centers draw ire for consuming vast energy
resources to fuel an artificial intelligence boom viewed with increased
skepticism. They have spiked utility bills, guzzled the region's fresh water,
occupied large tracts of land, and emitted a hum so constant that some
residents have sued over excessive noise.

The projects have sparked renewed civic engagement in rural areas and small
towns--stories that inspire David and Goliath comparisons. Residents ignite
with fury upon finding out their local elected officials have made deals in
the dark to bring data centers to town. They come out in force to city council
meetings, zoning hearings, and protests in an effort to confront the power of
major utility companies and multinational tech corporations with billions of
dollars at their disposal.

This growing opposition has forced Michigan's elected officials to reconsider
the wisdom of the state's 2024 decision to hand out tax breaks to data center
constructors.

Abdul El-Sayed, an epidemiologist and former Wayne County public health
official running in the August 4 Democratic primary for U.S. Senate, told Barn
Raiser that the corporations building data centers aren't straightforward
about their development plans.

"There's been so little transparency on the part of the corporations
themselves and the part of the utilities," he said. "It has raised the hackles
of folks who've learned not to trust a lot of these bigger corporations when
they tell them everything's going to be okay."

El-Sayed is locked in a fierce contest that has accentuated divides within the
Democratic Party. El-Sayed, whose parents immigrated from Egypt, has pledged
not to accept corporate PAC money, has called for eliminating arms sales to
Israel and supports universal health care and abolishing Immigration and
Customs Enforcement (ICE). Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) is a vocal supporter
of Israel who has accepted money from corporate PACs, outside groups like the
American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) and has the support of
Democratic party leader Sen. Chuck Schumer. Michigan state Sen. Mallory
McMorrow, a third challenger in the race, suspended her campaign July 5.

An April Emerson College poll shows data centers could be among the deciding
issues in the election. Emerson's poll of 519 likely Michigan primary voters
found that a majority, or 55%, opposed data centers being built in or near
their community, versus 27% who supported them. Opposition to data centers was
much higher among likely Democratic primary voters, with 63% opposed versus
45% among likely Republican primary voters.

Dark money spending and support for Israel remains another flashpoint in the
campaign, gaining national attention. The Associated Press
[reported](https://apnews.com/article/aipac-michigan-senate-stevens-
elsayed-588bb869eb557643950bf68d6a0d7a10) AIPAC and its affiliated groups have
spent close to $30 million backing Stevens, which is their largest investment
ever in a single race.

In January, El-Sayed released a [terms of engagement
proposal](https://abdulforsenate.com/2026/01/datacenters/) for data centers,
which includes a guarantee for local jobs, a freeze on consumer electricity
rate hikes and community benefit agreements. In recent weeks, he has shown
support for a system of federal oversight and public ownership of AI
companies, a proposal first advanced by Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), who has
endorsed El-Sayed.

Stevens has not laid out any similar positions. At a Democratic primary debate
in July, Stevens connected data center construction with job creation,
[saying](https://finance-commerce.com/2026/07/michigan-ai-data-center-local-
opposition/) it will put Michigan "on the forefront of innovation and
manufacturing," but she has also called for protecting Michiganders from data
center costs.

In an email statement to Barn Raiser, Stevens wrote, "When it comes to data
centers and AI infrastructure, my top priority is making sure costs don't go
up for Michigan families and that we are protecting good-paying union jobs. We
cannot allow utility companies like DTE to pass new costs onto consumers while
these projects move forward."

Stevens did not answer the question regarding Michigan residents' concern
about AI potentially resulting in less jobs.

" Part of the problem with our politics is too often corporations are buying
and selling politicians in the first place. In the case of DTE, our local
utility, they've given to 93% of state legislators," said El-Sayed,
referencing McMorrow, who eventually dropped out. DTE was McMorrow's [top
donor](https://michiganadvance.com/2026/04/28/michigan-u-s-senate-primary-
tightens-as-mcmorrow-el-sayed-outpace-stevens-in-q1-fundraising/) in her 2022
state Senate reelection campaign. El-Sayed's current opponent, Stevens, has
[received
money](https://www.fec.gov/data/receipts/?data_type=processed&committee_id=C00638650&committee_id=C00746735&committee_id=C00903039&committee_id=C00906933&contributor_name=C00081547)
from DTE since her first U.S. House reelection campaign in 2020.

McMorrow was among the 38 state senators to vote for a Senate bill that
exempted hyperscale data centers from sales and use taxes on their equipment.
The bill was signed into law by Democratic Gov. Gretchen Whitmer in 2025.

In hindsight, El-Sayed said a more extensive review process should have
occurred before state legislators approved laws to entice data center
development in the state.

"I think we should have spent a bit more time to hold the particular utilities
accountable ahead of laying out the red carpet, as our state has done," he
said.

Data centers have split support amongst unions and their endorsements. The
United Auto Workers (UAW), which has over 400,000 members nationwide, endorsed
El-Sayed in June. In an April press conference with Bernie Sanders and other
labor leaders, UAW president Shawn Fain compared AI to NAFTA because of the
risks it poses to workers and communities. "The same greedy corporate power
brokers today want us to believe that killing millions of jobs in the name of
AI will be a good thing, and the working class knows better," he said. Several
of the building trades unions, on the other hand, view data centers as a
catalyst for job creation, with many, including Plumbers Local 98 and
Pipefitters, Steamfitters, Refrigeration & Air Conditioning Service Local
Union 636, having endorsed Stevens.

Michigan's chapter of the AFL-CIO, the nation's largest federation of labor
unions, has not made an endorsement in the Senate race. In June, the AFL-CIO
released a [policy agenda for the next five
years](https://aflcio.org/press/releases/following-constitutional-convention-
afl-cio-releases-labor-movements-agenda-build). It included demands that data
centers and AI infrastructure be "built by and run on union labor," while
requiring that "data centers pay their fair share of costs and taxes" and that
working-class families and communities "are protected and included every step
of the way, including regulations over water and power use."

Construction workers may be the only local residents who stand to benefit from
the data center boom. A Citizens Research Council of Michigan
[report](https://crcmich.org/PUBLICAT/2020s/2026/rpt426-data_centers_in_Michigan.pdf)
on data centers found that the economic benefits of data centers largely occur
during the construction phase and concluded that the projects aren't long-term
drivers of economic development. In June, _Bloomberg_
[reported](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-06-01/us-construction-
spending-on-data-centers-eclipses-50-billion) that data centers account for
2.3% of all construction spending in the United States.

In a July [debate](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XE5V0RjWLAI&t=3s), El-Sayed
and Stevens clashed over their approaches to AI and data centers. El-Sayed
reiterated his community engagement plan and added, "I think we have to be
serious about the fact that these pose real dangers," he said. "And the people
who are pushing them are the richest, most powerful corporate CEOs in the
history of our economy."

Stevens did not speak directly to citizens' concerns about AI but pledged to
entice data centers to pay for utilities and rate increases. "I also want to
secure Michigan being on the forefront of innovation," she said in a statement
to Barn Raiser.

Michigan state Rep. Dylan Wegela (D-Garden City) voted against the tax breaks
for data centers when the Michigan House of Representatives voted on the bill
in 2023. Wegela had concerns about the environmental impact of data centers
from the beginning, he said, but hadn't anticipated the magnitude of the
pushback against using hyperscale facilities to drive AI developments.

"I think there are a lot of concerns with that industry right now and concerns
about what the technology, unregulated as it is now, might do to working-class
people," Wegela said. "And I think that is one of the many reasons this is
becoming so controversial now."

For Wegela, data centers are an issue that unites people across party lines.
"In areas that these data centers are coming to, you have these coalitions of
people on the left and the right coming out to fight together against data
centers," he said. "That's working class versus Big Tech."

That coalition of residents was on display on a sunny Saturday morning in
Traverse City, Michigan. About 40 protesters showed up to oppose data center
construction across Michigan, one of several anti-data center protests that
took place across the state on April 11. At the Traverse City protest,
attendees brought signs decrying data centers and signs in support of Lake
Michigan's freshwater supply. Speakers voiced their opposition to AI in
schools and expressed skepticism about the number of local jobs that data
centers would generate.

post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fac36c7bd-7c15-4e39-b0da-7a4eb42198dd_1200x772.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!0aJP!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fac36c7bd-7c15-4e39-b0da-7a4eb42198dd_1200x772.jpeg)Ryan
Wagner, the Kalkaska County GOP party chair, speaks at an anti-data center
rally in April in Traverse City, Michigan. _(Miles MacClure)_

Ryan Wagner, the Kalkaska County GOP party chair, appeared alongside Mitch
Distin, who helped organize the protest and is running as a Democrat for state
representative in Michigan's 104th district.

Wagner voiced his discontent with the Make America Great Again movement after
continuous campaign promises broken by the Trump administration, like
financial gain for working-class Americans, and he found common ground with
Democrats seeking to maintain natural resources and oppose AI companies. "I
feed my kids off this land. I don't want Big Tech to poison it," Wagner told
the crowd.

In November, a company called Rocklocker--a subsidiary of oil and gas company
Reefworks--proposed building a data center in rural Kalkaska County, just east
of Traverse City, on 1,440 acres of land owned by the Michigan Department of
Natural Resources. But community backlash was fierce. At meetings to discuss
the proposal, residents didn't buy the economic benefits claimed by Rocklocker
and they were wary of the environmental impact.

"The scientific literature is abundantly clear that none of the benefits are
distributed or trickle down to local communities, they're the ones who
ultimately pay the price for data centers," Distin told the protestors. "The
only people who are benefiting from this are big tech CEOs and the
legislators."

If a data center is abandoned by a company, it's unclear who will be
responsible to pick up the pieces. "What happens if the company goes
bankrupt?" said Wegela. "You've seen factories across the state for the
automotive industry and cities have been on the hook for cleaning those up or
maintaining those. And I just think these are things that aren't being talked
about enough."

"Democrats should be leading the opposition to unchecked data center growth,"
said Michelle Deatrick, chair of the DNC Climate Council. "That's not because
we oppose technology, it's because we believe growth needs to serve the public
interest, it needs to serve the people, and that's in both the short and the
long term."

One tactic used by local organizers has been to implement moratoriums. For
instance, residents in Livingston County, north of Detroit, [successfully
pushed](https://barnraisingmedia.com/data-centers-are-reshaping-local-
politics-in-the-great-lakes/) Howell Township to approve a six-month
moratorium on data center projects, including the $1 billion, 1,077-acre data
center proposed backed by Meta, which owns Facebook.

Michigan State Rep. Jennifer Wortz, a Republican in the 35th District,
[introduced a
bill](https://www.legislature.mi.gov/documents/2025-2026/billintroduced/House/pdf/2026-HIB-5594.pdf)
in February that would place a moratorium on data center construction across
the state until April 2027.

Towns, counties, cities, and states across the country are deciding how to
respond. An analysis from The Information found more than [300 bans or
moratoriums](https://www.theinformation.com/articles/300-plus-bans-
moratoriums-threatening-u-s-data-center-
boom?utm_campaign=Editorial&utm_content=Article&utm_medium=organic_social&utm_source=bluesky%2Cthreads%2Ctwitter)
across the United States.
([Datacenterbans.com](https://www.datacenterbans.com/) has an interactive map
and updates a tracker on data center policy around the country.) On July 14,
New York enacted the nation's first statewide one-year moratorium on data
center construction following an executive order signed by Gov. Kathy Hochul.
Maine nearly became the first state to do so in April, when the state
legislature [passed a moratorium](https://dailyyonder.com/maine-is-set-to-ban-
data-centers-becoming-the-first-state-in-the-nation-to-do-so/2026/04/15/), but
Gov. Janet Mills, a Democrat, vetoed the bill.

As communities sour on data center projects, they're also turning away from
AI. A [Quinnipiac University poll](https://poll.qu.edu/poll-
release?releaseid=3955) from March 2026 found that 81% of millennials were
concerned about AI. The poll also found that 55% of Americans believe AI will
do more harm than good, up from 44% in April 2025.

" I don't know if everybody in the public space has connected that the data
center and the AI fight is one and the same," said Wegela.

In the workplace, AI is meeting resistance. Futurism
[reported](https://futurism.com/artificial-intelligence/zoomers-ai-sabotage)
that some workers are intentionally sabotaging their employer's AI
deployments. Fears over the direction of AI are also turning violent. In
April, a Houston man traveled to San Francisco and [hurled a Molotov cocktail
](https://sfstandard.com/2026/04/13/sam-altman-home-molotov-cocktail-shooting-
suspects/)at OpenAI CEO Sam Altman's house.

"The fear and anxiety about AI is justified," Altman wrote on his
[blog](https://blog.samaltman.com/2279512) in the wake of the attack. "We are
in the process of witnessing the largest change to society in a long time, and
perhaps ever."

Kyle Blomquist, an architect running for Congress in Michigan's rural 1st
congressional district, said the data center tax breaks handed out by Michigan
should be repealed. "I'm surprised by the fact that our state has decided to
incentivize the location of data centers in the state through these various
different tax abatement programs and cuts," said Blomquist.

When Michigan first legalized medical marijuana, local governments had to set
ordinances about marijuana store zoning before any business was allowed to set
up shop. Blomquist said he would have liked to see a similar process play out
with data centers.

Instead, the Wild West of data center growth has exposed a need for towns and
counties to update their zoning ordinances. Many of the towns where data
centers have been proposed have never had such large developments set up shop
before.

" I would've liked more caution with the data centers, more along those lines
where you give the communities the opportunity to set their own conditions as
to whether or not they want them located there at all," said Blomquist.
"Instead, it's kind of a free-for-all."

_Miles MacClure is a writer based in Traverse City, Michigan._****_This story
was first published by Barn Raiser, whose coverage was supported by a grant
from the[ Lumpkin Family Foundation](https://www.lumpkinfoundation.org/)._
